sentences.text: What is the dot product?
Let's see what it is, why it's built this way, and what it tells us about the wind.
A vector is an arrow, with a length and a direction.
Vector a goes five steps right and one up, and vector b goes one right and three up.
sentences.audio_text: Vector [A](/ˈA/) goes five steps right and one up, and vector b goes one right and three up.

sentences.text: These numbers are called components: five and one are the components of vector a and one and three are those of vector b.
sentences.audio_text: These numbers are called components: five and one are the components of vector [A](/ˈA/) and one and three are those of vector b.

sentences.text: Pythagoras' theorem gives their lengths, written with two straight bars: about five point one and three point one six.
So how do we find the dot product?
We multiply the matching components, and then add.
Arrows in three-dimensional space have three components, along x, y and z, so we'd add three products.
Ours lie flat, in two dimensions, so the third term drops out.
The first components give five times one, which is five, and the second give one times three, which is three.
Adding them, a dot b equals eight: a single number, not an arrow.
sentences.audio_text: Adding them, [A](/ˈA/) dot b equals eight: a single number, not an arrow.

sentences.text: A number like this is called a scalar, so the dot product is also called the scalar product.
Now let's look at how the angle between the two arrows plays a role.
The dot product can also be written as the two lengths times the cosine of theta, the angle between them.
The cosine is one when two arrows point the same way, zero at a right angle, and minus one when they point in opposite directions.
Here theta is about sixty degrees, with a cosine of about point five.
Multiplied out, that's eight again, and we'll call this equation one.
Let's keep one arrow fixed in all three pictures, and change only the other one.
The fixed arrow, p, has components three and zero.
First, q has components two and zero, pointing the same way as p: three times two plus zero times zero is six, a positive number.
Next, q has components zero and two, at a right angle to p, and both products are zero.
When two vectors are at right angles, their dot product is zero.
Last, q has components minus two and zero, pointing in the opposite direction: three times minus two is minus six, a negative number.
So the dot product measures how much two arrows point the same way.
Now let's find a picture for the dot product.
From the tip of vector a we drop a line onto b's line, at a right angle.
sentences.audio_text: From the tip of vector [A](/ˈA/) we drop a line onto b's line, at a right angle.

sentences.text: The piece it marks off is called the shadow of vector a on b.
sentences.audio_text: The piece it marks off is called the shadow of vector [A](/ˈA/) on b.

sentences.text: In this right triangle, the shadow is the length of vector a times cos theta.
sentences.audio_text: In this right triangle, the shadow is the length of vector [A](/ˈA/) times cos theta.

sentences.text: Divide both sides of equation one by the length of b, and only the shadow is left on the right: eight over three point one six, or two point five three.
There's another way to reach the same shadow.
Divide b by its own length to get b hat, the unit vector along b: length one, same direction.
Its components are one and three, each divided by three point one six.
Dividing b by its length divides the dot product by it too, so a dot b hat is the shadow itself: two point five three again.
sentences.audio_text: Dividing b by its length divides the dot product by it too, so [A](/ˈA/) dot b hat is the shadow itself: two point five three again.

sentences.text: So the dot product is the shadow times the length of b.
But why not stop at the shadow?
There are three good reasons.
The first is that the order shouldn't matter.
The shadow of vector a on b is two point five three, but the shadow of b on vector a is one point five seven.
sentences.audio_text: The shadow of vector [A](/ˈA/) on b is two point five three, but the shadow of b on vector [A](/ˈA/) is one point five seven.

sentences.text: Multiply each by the length of the arrow it falls on, and both give eight.
The second reason is practical: it's quick to calculate, with no angle and no square root.
Suppose the wind blows towards the north-east at ten metres per second.
Written as a vector, v has components six and eight.
How much of this wind blows towards the east?
To find out, we take the dot product of v with the unit vector pointing east, x hat, whose components are one and zero.
Then v dot x hat is six times one, plus eight times zero, which is six.
So six metres per second is the eastward part of the wind.
It's simply the first component: a dot product with a unit vector picks out the part of v along it.
The third reason is that physics often needs both sizes.
Pull a sled with a force vector, F, of twenty newtons, tilted sixty degrees up, while it moves along a displacement vector, d.
The upward part of the pull does no work; the part along the ground, the shadow of F on d, is ten newtons.
Work, in joules, is that force times the distance: fifty joules if d is five metres.
If d doubles to ten metres, the work doubles to one hundred joules, but the shadow is still ten newtons.
So the shadow alone can't give the work: we must multiply by the length of d, and the dot product does exactly that.
Now let's look at how the dot product is used in weather.
Imagine one thermometer fixed on a pole.
How fast its temperature changes over time is called the local rate, written partial T by partial t.
Partial means only time changes; the place stays fixed.
A second thermometer rides a balloon drifting with the wind, inside one air parcel: a small volume of air that moves with the flow.
Its rate, following the air parcel, is written capital D T by D t.
Here is the equation the balloon's thermometer obeys.
It tells us how anything the air carries, called phi, like temperature or moisture, changes as we follow an air parcel.
On the left is the change following the parcel.
On the right is the change at one fixed place, plus a term with v, the wind, and grad, which we'll meet soon.
Advection means being carried along by the flow, so this advection term is the change from being carried to places where phi is different.
The left side is called the material derivative.
It isn't a partial derivative, because the place moves with the parcel: it's the partial derivative plus the advection term.
For temperature, that term is v dot grad T, and its dot is our dot product.
To see it at work, picture a map where the temperature rises one degree for every hundred kilometres east, and doesn't change as you walk north.
Join the places with the same temperature right now, and you get straight north to south lines, one every hundred kilometres.
These are called isotherms.
Walk east, and each isotherm you cross is one degree warmer: that's partial T by partial x, the change going east only.
Walk north, and you stay on one isotherm, so partial T by partial y is zero.
These two rates form one arrow: the temperature gradient, read grad T.
A kelvin step is the same size as a degree Celsius step, so grad T is ten to the minus five kelvin per metre going east, and zero going north.
It points the way the temperature increases fastest: straight across the isotherms, towards warmer air.
Now a wind blows across the map, the one carrying our balloon: ten metres per second, at sixty degrees to grad T.
Its shadow on grad T, ten times cos sixty, is five metres per second, straight across the isotherms.
The other part, ten times sine sixty, is eight point six six metres per second along them, and moving along an isotherm brings no temperature change.
The length of grad T, by Pythagoras, is the square root of ten to the minus five squared, plus zero squared: just ten to the minus five kelvin per metre.
So v dot grad T is the wind's shadow times the length of grad T: five metres per second times ten to the minus five kelvin per metre.
The metres cancel, leaving five times ten to the minus five kelvin per second, or point one eight kelvin per hour.
What does point one eight kelvin per hour mean?
It's a rate in time, while one degree per hundred kilometres is a rate in space.
Think of the map as a snapshot, and look at the pole.
Its air comes from upwind, where the wind comes from: down and to the left, on the colder side.
The air that reaches it in an hour is now eighteen kilometres upwind across the isotherms, so it's point one eight degrees colder.
But the snapshot doesn't stay still.
Suppose each air parcel keeps its temperature: no sunshine and no mixing.
Then the balloon's reading never changes, so capital D T by D t is zero.
And since the air carries its temperature along, the whole pattern of isotherms slides with the wind.
Our wind is the same everywhere, so the lines move east, eighteen kilometres every hour.
Now let's start the clock again and watch both thermometers.
As the isotherms slide past, the pole reads thirteen, then twelve point eight two after one hour, twelve point six four after two, and twelve point four six after three.
That's the colder air from upwind arriving.
Meanwhile the balloon moves with its parcel, so it stays at thirteen degrees.
Our equation says the same.
Put zero for capital D T by D t, and subtract v dot grad T from both sides: partial T by partial t equals minus v dot grad T.
The wind has a part towards warmer air, so v dot grad T is plus point one eight kelvin per hour.
The minus sign makes it a fall of point one eight at the pole, as colder air is carried in.
So why does the balloon stay at thirteen?
In one hour it moves eighteen kilometres across the isotherms, to where the map read thirteen point one eight an hour ago.
Crossing the isotherms like that is worth plus point one eight: that's the advection term.
But in that hour every place has cooled by point one eight degrees, and that fall, minus point one eight, is the local rate.
They cancel, so the balloon still reads thirteen.
Now let's change only the map: the temperature rises one degree every fifty kilometres, instead of every hundred.
The isotherms are twice as close, so grad T doubles, to two times ten to the minus five kelvin per metre.
Its length, by Pythagoras again, is that same number, because the northward part is still zero.
The wind's shadow is still five metres per second.
But the dot product doubles, to point three six kelvin per hour, so the pole cools twice as fast.
Just as with the sled, the shadow stayed the same, so on its own it would miss this change.
Multiplying by the length of grad T catches it.
To sum up, the dot product multiplies matching components and adds, giving a number, not an arrow.
In pictures, it's the shadow of one arrow on the other, times the other's length.
When the arrows point the same way, it's positive.
At right angles, it's zero.
In opposite directions, it's negative.
With a unit vector, it picks out one part of an arrow.
And in physics, it gives the work a force does, and how fast the wind changes the temperature at a fixed place.
